q: If Cao Shuang had followed Huan Fan's advice, could the Incident at the Gaoping Tombs have been avoided?
reply:
## What the sources actually say

The core account is in the *Wei Shu*, biography of Cao Shuang (曹爽) and his associates:

- **Jiaping 1 (249), 1st month, day jiawu**: the emperor (Qi Wang Fang, 曹芳) went to pay respects at Gaoping Tomb; Cao Shuang and his brothers all accompanied him. Sima Yi (司马宣王) deployed troops, first seized the arsenal, then camped at the pontoon bridge over the Luo River, and submitted a memorial accusing Cao Shuang of betraying the regency and harboring treasonous designs [18].
- **Huan Fan's advice**: hearing of the coup, Huan Fan forged an edict, forced the Pingchang gate open, and fled south to Cao Shuang. "Huan Fan urged Cao Shuang to have the imperial carriage go to Xu Chang and summon outside troops." To Cao Xi he pressed: "Your other camp is right near the palace gate to the south, and the Luoyang diannong office is outside the city — you can call them at will. Going to Xu Chang now takes only one night's stay; the separate stores at Xu Chang are enough to supply weapons. What you should worry about is grain — and the Grand Minister of Agriculture's seal is on my person." [1][2]
- **Sima Yi's and Jiang Ji's reaction**: "When Huan Fan came out to join Cao Shuang, Sima Xuan-wang said to Jiang Ji: 'The brains have gone over.' Jiang Ji said: 'Huan Fan is clever, but a nag loves the beans in its manger — Cao Shuang will surely not use his plan.'" (09-0027n1, quoting Gan Bao's *Jin Shu*)
- **The surrender**: Xu Yun and Chen Tai urged Cao Shuang to go confess early. Jiang Ji sent a letter conveying Sima Yi's intent, and Yin Damu swore by the Luo River that only dismissal from office was intended. Cao Shuang believed it, disbanded, and said "I can still be a rich man at home." Huan Fan wept: "Cao Zidan [Cao Zhen] was a fine man — and begot you brothers, you calves!" (*Wei Shi Chunqiu*, 09-0027n1)

## What this does and does not support

**Grounds for thinking it could have been avoided:**

- Sima Yi's own remark ("the brains have gone over") and Jiang Ji's "Cao Shuang will surely not use his plan" are, on their face, admissions that Huan Fan's plan was a serious threat — otherwise there was nothing to fear.
- The plan rested on the strongest asset Cao Shuang had: possession of the emperor's person. Huan Fan's argument — "you and the Son of Heaven are together; you can order the empire, who would dare not respond?" — is the classic logic of "holding the emperor to command the realm."
- The material elements he named were real: the Luoyang diannong office outside the walls, the separate arsenal at Xu Chang, and his own control of the agriculture ministry's seal for grain.

**Grounds for thinking it would not have saved him:**

- **Sima Yi had already taken the decisive physical assets**: the arsenal, the city gates, and the Luo River bridge, and he acted under a decree of the Empress Dowager (永宁宫), i.e., with the apparatus of legitimacy on his side. Cao Shuang's brothers' offices — Cao Xi as 中领军, Cao Xun as 武卫将军 — meant their troops were inside Luoyang, which Sima Yi had sealed.
- **Cao Shuang's household was in Luoyang**, in Sima Yi's hands (his wife Lady Liu is shown at the mansion in *Shi Yu*, 09-0026n1). That is a powerful reason to surrender, though the sources do not state it as his motive.
- **Cao Shuang's standing was poor**: the Luogu campaign disaster, the extravagance, the exclusion of Sima Yi, the resentment of officials. Contemporaries judged accordingly — Xin Xianying (辛宪英) told her brother, "Cao Shuang's talent is no match for the Grand Tutor's" [22].
- **Later precedents are discouraging**: Wang Ling (王凌) tried essentially this — to set up Cao Biao with Xu Chang as capital — and failed [10]. So did Guanqiu Jian and Zhuge Dan. The "go to Xu Chang, summon the provinces" formula was not a reliable winner.
- Huan Fan himself was a marginal figure: "Cao Shuang respected him as an old worthy of his home commandery, but was not very close to him" [13]. He was not inside the decision-making circle.

## Bottom line

The *Sanguozhi* does not answer the counterfactual, and no source claims Cao Shuang would have won. What the record does establish is that Sima Yi and Jiang Ji treated Huan Fan's plan as the one thing worth worrying about, that it had a coherent military and legitimacy logic, and that Cao Shuang's refusal was attributed to character — "a nag loves the beans in its manger" — rather than to any demonstrated impossibility. At the same time, the plan required a fight Sima Yi was better positioned to wage: he held Luoyang, the arsenal, the gates, the empress dowager's mandate, and Cao Shuang's family. So the most defensible reading is: **the plan offered a real chance of resistance and possibly of survival or a prolonged civil war, but "avoiding the Incident" outright — i.e., defeating Sima Yi — is far from demonstrated, and the sources lean toward the view that Cao Shuang's temperament, not the plan's merits, decided the outcome.**

One caution on detail: the exact dates (Jiaping 1 = 249; day jiawu, and the execution following the Zhang Dang case) come from the *Qi Wang* annals [9]; Huan Fan's precise route and the number of men involved are given only in Pei's supplementary notes, not in Chen Shou's main text.

q: Li Yan and Zhuge Liang were both regents named in Liu Bei's deathbed charge — so why was Zhuge Liang able to demote Li Yan to a commoner?
reply:
A small correction to the premise first: 《三国志·蜀书·先主传》records the deathbed arrangement as "托孤于丞相亮，尚书令李严为副" — Zhuge Liang was the principal, Li Yan the deputy (副). Li Yan's 《李严传》also says the two "并受遗诏辅少主," but adds that Li Yan was made 中都护、统内外军事 and was left to garrison 永安, i.e., he was stationed away from the capital, whereas Zhuge Liang as 丞相录尚书事 ran the government at Chengdu.

That said, the demotion was not simply a matter of Zhuge Liang's power; Li Yan was removed for a specific, documented offense and through a formal process.

**The offense (建兴九年, 231, the 祁山 campaign)**
Li Yan (then renamed Li Ping) was in charge of transporting supplies. Heavy rains came, the grain ran out, and Li Yan sent 参军狐忠 and 督军成藩 to summon Zhuge Liang back; Zhuge Liang withdrew accordingly. Li Yan then pretended to be astonished — "军粮饶足，何以便归!" — trying to shift the blame for his own failure onto Zhuge Liang and to make it look as if Zhuge Liang had needlessly retreated; he also memorialized the throne that the army had retreated feignedly to lure the enemy. Zhuge Liang produced the entire file of Li Yan's own handwritten letters and memorials, "平违错章灼," and Li Yan had nothing to say and admitted his guilt [22].

**The process**
Zhuge Liang then submitted a memorial to the throne listing Li Yan's earlier conduct — doing out small favors while 安身求名, refusing to bring his troops to Hanzhong, demanding 五郡 to be made 巴州刺史, and citing Sima Yi's opening a 府 to angle for advantage — and concluded that the situation could not be tolerated ("不可苞含，以危大业"). The removal was carried out by a collective memorial to the 尚书, signed by a long roster of senior figures: 刘琰, 魏延, 袁綝, 吴壹, 高翔, 吴班, 杨仪, 邓芝, 刘巴, 费祎, 姜维 and many others, resolving to "解平任，免官禄、节传、印绶、符策，削其爵土" [23]. So it was formally a judicial/administrative act of the Shu government, not a private act of Zhuge Liang.

**Why Li Yan could not resist it**
- The evidence was in Li Yan's own hand, and he himself confessed ("辞穷情竭，首谢罪负").
- The decision was backed by the whole senior establishment, including the men who would have been his potential allies.
- Li Yan's power base was local (江州), and he had already been maneuvered out of it: Zhuge Liang had memorialized to make Li Yan's son Li Feng 江州都督督军 in his place, and Li Yan himself was brought to Hanzhong to "以中都护署府事" [12].

**Aftermath**
Li Yan was reduced to commoner status and moved to 梓潼郡, not executed. Zhuge Liang wrote to Li Feng reassuring him that the family's position remained honorable and that "否可复通，逝可复还" — i.e., restoration was possible if Li Yan mended his ways [24]. Li Yan hoped Zhuge Liang would personally restore him and, judging that no successor could, died of illness in 建兴十二年 (234) upon hearing of Zhuge Liang's death [22]. 习凿齿's comment in Pei's note praises this as "善于用刑," noting Li Yan bore no resentment [7].

So the short answer: he was not "demoted" by an act of will between two equal regents; he was convicted, on documentary evidence and by his own admission, of obstructing and falsifying a military campaign, and the punishment was imposed by a collective government decision that the entire senior officer corps endorsed.

q: Should Xiahou Ba have defected to Shu Han?
reply:
The sources don't frame this as a question of "should," so any answer has to be an assessment built from what they record. Here is what《三国志》and裴松之's notes give us.

**Why he went**

Xiahou Ba (夏侯霸), son of Xiahou Yuan, was a man who "always ground his teeth" against Shu, since Shu had killed his father at Dingjun Mountain [3]. He was a favorite of Cao Shuang, serving in the Zhengshi era as 讨蜀护军、右将军、博昌亭侯 [1]. When Sima Yi destroyed Cao Shuang in 249 (嘉平元年, 04-0016), 《魏略》says he had two reasons to flee:

- He heard Cao Shuang was killed and that his own nephew Xiahou Xuan had been summoned east, and "thought the disaster would surely spread to him; his heart was already frightened" [3].
- He had previously been on bad terms with the Yongzhou governor Guo Huai, and now Guo Huai replaced Xiahou Xuan as 征西 — "Xiahou Ba was even more uneasy, so he fled to Shu" [3].

Chen Shou's own text says simply: "Hearing Shuang was executed, he doubted his own safety and fled into Shu" (聞爽誅，自疑，亡入蜀, 09-0008).

**What staying might have meant**

His relative Xiahou Xuan did not flee — 《魏氏春秋》records that Xiahou Ba called to Xiahou Xuan to come along, and Xuan refused: "How could I live on ignobly, lodging myself among bandits?" [23]. Xiahou Xuan stayed, was repeatedly demoted, became involved in the Li Feng plot of 254 (嘉平六年), and was handed to the commandant of justice on a charge of 大逆无道 [26]. So the man who stayed was eventually destroyed anyway. Against that, the Wei court, "on account of Xiahou Yuan's old merit," pardoned Xiahou Ba's sons and merely banished them to Lelang — it did not treat the flight as a capital crime for the family [1].

**What he gained in Shu**

He was well received, and there was a real family tie: his cousin (夏侯霸從妹), taken by Zhang Fei around 200, bore a daughter who became Liu Shan's empress — so Liu Shan's sons were Xiahou relatives. Liu Shan reassured him: "Your father died in the ranks; it was not my forebears' own hand," and pointed to his son, saying "this is a Xiahou nephew" [3]. In Shu he rose to 车骑将军 [17] and campaigned with Jiang Wei against Guo Huai [15]. He also gave a sharp forecast — that Sima Yi would busy himself building up his family and that Zhong Hui was the future danger to Wu and Shu [2].

**Assessment**

On the record, the flight looks *reasonable* rather than dishonorable: the purge was real, his patron was dead, his nephew was being recalled, his enemy Guo Huai was taking command over him, and the alternative course (staying, like Xiahou Xuan) ended in execution. He was not abandoning a stable regime — he was reacting to a coup that had just killed his faction. His prediction about Zhong Hui also proved accurate, which the sources cite approvingly.

Two caveats. First, the sources describe his motive as fear and self-doubt, not principle; 《魏氏春秋》has Xiahou Xuan voice the opposing view that fleeing to Shu meant "living on ignobly among bandits." Second, that the Wei court only exiled his sons suggests he may not have been in immediate mortal danger at the moment he ran. So "should" depends on whether one weighs prudence and survival (which favor going) against loyalty to Wei and the shame of serving the state that killed his father (which favor staying). The text itself does not condemn him; it presents a frightened man with good reason to be frightened, who read the situation correctly.

If you want, I can pull the fuller passage on Xiahou Xuan's fall to lay the comparison out in more detail.

q: In the year Ma Su lost Chieh-t'ing, which year of which reign era was Shu-Han using? What year was it on the Wei side? And what year is that in the Western calendar?
reply:
According to the *San guo zhi* record of the Chieh-t'ing campaign:

- **Shu-Han:** 建興 (Jianxing) 6th year — 「建興六年春……與郃戰于街亭」 (諸葛亮傳, 35-0011); also 「建興六年，屬參軍馬謖先鋒……大敗於街亭」 (王平傳, 43-0012).
- **Wei:** 太和 (Taihe) 2nd year — 「太和二年，蜀相諸葛亮出祁山，遣將軍馬謖至街亭」 (郭淮傳, 26-0026).
- **Western calendar:** AD 228 (both 建興六年 of Shu-Han and 太和二年 of Wei = 228).

So the same year was Shu-Han's Jianxing 6 and Wei's Taihe 2 (the Wei emperor then being Mingdi, 曹叡), i.e. 228 CE.

q: Chen Shou was born in Shu, so why does the Records of the Three Kingdoms contain so few accounts of Shu's deeds?
reply:
**Short answer: Chen Shou says it himself — it is not that he slighted Shu, but that Shu kept no historical records to work from.**

**1. Chen Shou's own explanation.** In his appraisal of the Later Ruler Liu Shan at the end of the *Shu Shu* [1], Chen Shou writes:

> 又國不置史，注記無官，是以行事多遺，災異靡書。諸葛亮雖達於為政，凡此之類，猶有未周焉。

"Moreover the state did not establish a history office, and there were no officials charged with records; therefore its deeds were largely lost and its portents and anomalies went unrecorded. Zhuge Liang, though thoroughly versed in government, was still not complete in matters of this kind."

So Chen Shou attributes the thinness of the Shu record to the absence of an official historiography in Shu, not to any lack of diligence or any bias of his own.

**2. This is consistent with the structure of the book.** The *Records* runs to 30 juan of Wei, 15 of Shu, 20 of Wu — Shu is by far the shortest section, exactly what you would expect if Shu produced the least documentation. Chen Shou's material on Shu came largely from non-official sources: he was himself from Shu (Ba commandery, a student of Qiao Zhou — see 42-0026, where Chen Shou narrates his farewell visit to Qiao Zhou in 269 and calls him "my" teacher's circle), and he drew on works such as the *Shu Ji* 蜀記 and *Yi Bu Qi Jiu Zhuan* 益部耆舊傳 that he cites in the Pei notes. He even edited and submitted a collection of Zhuge Liang's writings to the Jin court (35-0035, dated 泰始十年 = 274).

**3. He flags the gaps explicitly rather than hiding them.** At Yang Xi's *Ji Han Fu Chen Zan* [37] he notes that some men who deserved record have no biography, and that he appends notes under Yang Xi's praises for those he could not give a *zhuan* to. In the *Xianzhu Zhuan* Pei Songzhi laments that the ancestral-temple regulations of Shu were "記載闕略" — lost for want of records [14].

**4. By contrast, Wei and Wu did have historiographical projects.** The Wu case is documented in Hua He's memorial [7]: Sun Quan in his last years ordered Ding Fu and Xiang Jun to compile a *Wu Shu*; under the boy-emperor Wei Yao, Zhou Zhao, Xue Ying, Liang Guang and Hua He were assigned to continue it, but the work stalled through deaths, exile and other misfortunes. Even so, the *Zhi Lin* cited by Pei notes that Sun Shao, Wu's first chancellor, has no biography because Wei Yao's history was compiled by a partisan faction [8] — showing the same problem in milder form.

**5. A related observation by Sun Sheng** [13]: "蜀少人士，故慈、潛等並見載述" — Shu had few eminent men, so even figures like Xu Ci and Hu Qian got entries. This cuts both ways: the small Shu talent pool is one reason minor Shu men appear at all, while the small pool of surviving documents is why major events are sometimes thinly covered.

So: Chen Shou being a Shu man is not the cause. If anything, his Shu origin gave him access to Shu materials (via Qiao Zhou's circle and local gazetteers) that a Wei or Wu writer would not have had. The cause he names is institutional — Shu had no history office, hence "行事多遺."

(Note: the exact date of Chen Shou's birth is not recorded in the *Sanguozhi*; his death is usually given as 297. I won't assert a birth year.)

q: When Liu Pei marched south from Chia-meng against Liu Chang, he left Huo Chün to hold the city. How long did Liu Chang's forces besiege it? How many soldiers did Huo Chün have, and how was the siege finally broken?
reply:
According to Huo Jun's biography in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (Shu shu 11, Huo Jun 霍峻, whose account is preserved only in Chen Shou's main text; there is no Pei Songzhi commentary attached to this passage):

- **Length of the siege:** "nearly a year" (且一年) — Liu Zhang's generals Fu Jin (扶禁) and Xiang Cun (向存) led over 10,000 men up the Lang River and besieged him, and for close to a year they could not take the city.
- **Huo Jun's force:** only a few hundred soldiers (城中兵才數百人).
- **How the siege was broken:** he waited until the besiegers grew slack and careless (伺其怠隙), then picked his best troops and sallied out, routing the enemy and cutting off Xiang Cun's head on the spot (即斬存首).

A related detail in the same passage: before this, Zhang Lu had sent his general Yang Bo (楊帛) to tempt Huo Jun into a joint defense of the city, and Huo Jun refused with the famous line, "My head you may have; the city you may not" (小人頭可得，城不可得).

Two caveats: the text says "nearly a year" without specifying months, and it gives the defenders as "only a few hundred" without a precise number, so no exact figures can be stated.

q: Ts'ao Ts'ao asked P'ei Ch'ien about Liu Pei's abilities. How did P'ei Ch'ien assess him?
reply:
这是《三国志·魏书·裴潜传》里的记载。曹操平定荆州后，任裴潜为参丞相军事，问他：「卿前与刘备俱在荆州，卿以备才略何如？」

q: P'ang Te killed Kuo Yüan with his own hand in the battle at P'ing-yang. According to P'ei Sung-chih's commentary, how was Kuo Yüan related to Chung Yao? And how did Chung Yao react when he saw the head — what did he say?
reply:
According to the Pei Sung-chih commentary (quoting the *Wei-lüeh*), recorded under P'ang Te's biography in the *Wei shu* (chüan 18):

- **Relation:** Kuo Yüan was **Chung Yao's nephew** — specifically his *wai-sheng* (外甥), i.e. the son of Chung Yao's sister.
- **Chung Yao's reaction:** When P'ang Te afterwards drew the head out of his quiver (鞬), **Chung Yao wept (見之而哭)**. P'ang Te apologized to him, and Chung Yao replied:

> 「援雖我甥，乃國賊也。卿何謝之？」
> "Though Kuo Yüan was my nephew, he was a traitor to the state. Why should you apologize?"

The passage in full: P'ang Te had cut down a head without knowing it was Kuo Yüan's; after the battle everyone said Kuo Yüan was dead but his head could not be found. P'ang Te then produced the head from his quiver, and Chung Yao wept at the sight of it.

(Note: the main text of the *San-kuo chih* simply says P'ang Te "personally cut off Yüan's head"; the detail about the quiver, the weeping, and Chung Yao's words comes from the *Wei-lüeh* as quoted in Pei's commentary. Chung Yao's own biography records his plan to attack Kuo Yüan as he crossed the Fen River.)

q: How did Cao Pi's Empress Zhen die? Do the historical sources disagree about it?
reply:
## 陈寿《三国志》正文的记载

《魏书·后妃传》记甄后（文昭甄皇后，明帝生母）之死只有一句：

> 践阼之后，山阳公奉二女以嫔于魏，郭后、李、阴贵人并爱幸，后愈失意，有怨言。帝大怒，二年六月，遣使赐死，葬于邺。

即：曹丕称帝（黄初元年十月）之后，甄后失宠、口出怨言，曹丕大怒，**黄初二年（221）六月派使者赐她死**，葬在邺城。这是陈寿正文的说法——明确的"赐死"。

## 各家的分歧

**1）王沈《魏书》（裴注引）完全洗白。** 它说曹丕本要用玺书迎甄氏到行在立为皇后，甄氏三次上表谦让；"时盛暑，帝欲须秋凉乃更迎后。会后疾遂笃，夏六月丁卯，崩于邺。帝哀痛咨嗟，策赠皇后玺绶。"——即病死，且曹丕哀痛追赠。

裴松之直接驳斥了这段：

> 文帝之不立甄氏，及加杀害，事有明审。魏史若以为大恶邪，则宜隐而不言……而崇饰虚文乃至于是，异乎所闻于旧史。推此而言，其称卞、甄诸后言行之善，皆难以实论。

他认为曹丕不立甄氏为后并加以杀害是确凿事实，《魏书》是在粉饰；并因此推断《魏书》所载卞后、甄后诸后"言行之善"都不可信，陈寿删去这些是有道理的。

**2）鱼豢《魏略》（裴注引）** 讲明帝即位后追痛甄后之死，郭太后"以忧暴崩"；并说明帝幼时被甄后临终托付给李夫人，李夫人后来才说出甄后"见谮之祸，不获大敛，被发覆面"。

**3）习凿齿《汉晋春秋》（裴注引）** 说得更具体：甄后被杀是因郭后得宠，"及殡，令被发覆面，以糠塞口"；明帝知道后常怀愤恨，多次哭着追问甄后死状，郭后反问"先帝自杀，何以责问我"，明帝大怒，**逼杀郭后**，并命殡殓的人照甄后的样子办。

## 分歧小结

- **死因**：陈寿说"遣使赐死"；《魏书》说病死、曹丕哀痛——裴松之判定后者为虚饰，赐死一事"明审"。
- **死后待遇**：只有裴注所引《魏略》《汉晋春秋》提到"被发覆面、以糠塞口"这类细节，陈寿正文不载。
- **郭后之死也连带分歧**：《魏略》说郭太后"以忧暴崩"，《汉晋春秋》说被明帝逼杀，《魏书》则载有明帝为郭太后写的哀策（青龙三年三月葬首阳陵西），把郭后当慈母来哀悼。三者互相矛盾。

所以答案是：以陈寿正文为准，甄后是被曹丕赐死（黄初二年六月）；而《魏书》的"病死说"被裴松之明确斥为曲笔，裴注补充的"被发覆面、以糠塞口"等细节出自《魏略》《汉晋春秋》，属于裴注保存的异说。

q: Why did the Sun-Liu alliance keep quarreling over Jing Province, until Sun Quan finally stabbed Guan Yu in the back?
reply:
## Short answer

Because from the very beginning the alliance was a marriage of convenience between two men who each wanted the *whole* of the middle Yangzi, and the "loan" of Jing was never a real loan. Both sides had a defensible claim, neither would give up the province, and once Cao Cao's threat receded enough — and once Lu Su, the alliance's chief keeper, died — the arithmetic of "who holds the upper river" pointed straight at Guan Yu's back.

## 1. The province was the one thing neither could concede

Jing Province (around modern Hubei/Hunan) sat on the Yangzi between Sun Quan's base in the east and Liu Bei's new base in the west.

- For Sun Quan it was the **upstream of his own state**. Lü Meng states the logic bluntly: Guan Yu "is located on the upper reaches of our state, and that situation cannot last long" (居國上流，其勢難久, 54-0031). Whoever held Jing could sail down and take Jianye.
- For Liu Bei it was the hinge of the whole Longzhong plan — the springboard to Yi Province and Xiangyang — and his only territory before 214.

So this was never a border squabble; it was the strategic core of both states.

## 2. The "loan" was ambiguous from day one

The word "borrow" (借) hides a real disagreement about ownership.

- Liu Bei's case: after Red Cliffs he himself campaigned south and took the four commanderies (Wuling, Changsha, Guiyang, Lingling), then was pushed forward by his followers as Governor of Jing after Liu Qi died — i.e. he held it as Liu Biao's heir (32-0011).
- Sun Quan's case: Zhou Yu had taken Nan Commandery at Red Cliffs, and it was **Sun Quan who handed Liu Bei land** — first "the south-bank land" as a gift from Zhou Yu, then, when that was too small, Liu Bei "again borrowed several commanderies of Jing from Quan" [4]. Sun's people therefore treated Nan Commandery as a loan.

Lu Su persuaded Sun Quan to make the loan on cold-blooded grounds — not generosity but alliance-building: "Let us use Liu Bei to pacify it; to multiply Cao Cao's enemies and build our own faction is the best plan" [3]. Cao Cao's reaction — dropping his brush when he heard Sun Quan had given Liu Bei land to build on — shows how well he understood it [15].

Note the ambiguity was baked in: Sun Quan himself later called the loan Lu Su's "one shortcoming" (一短) — a shortcoming he forgave because of Lu Su's two great services [13].

## 3. The first real rupture: 215 (建安二十年)

Once Liu Bei took Yi Province, Sun Quan demanded the province back. Liu Bei stalled: "I am now planning for Liang Province; when Liang is settled, I will give you all of Jing." Sun Quan's verdict: "This is borrowing without returning, and using empty words to drag out the years" (此假而不反，而欲以虛辭引歳, 47-0012).

What followed was a near-war:

- Sun Quan appointed his own administrators to the three southern commanderies; Guan Yu drove them all out.
- Sun Quan sent Lü Meng with 20,000 men against Changsha, Lingling, and Guiyang; Lu Su with 10,000 at Baqiu to block Guan Yu; Sun Quan himself at Lukou.
- Liu Bei came down to Gong'an and sent Guan Yu with 30,000 to Yiyang.

The famous **single-sword meeting** (單刀俱會) at Yiyang is the alliance's argument in miniature. Guan Yu claimed the province by right of Liu Bei's blood and effort at Wulin. Lu Su answered: you had "less than a single regiment" at Changban, our ruler pitied you and grudged neither land nor men, and now "having got your hands on Yi Province, you want to carve up Jing as well — this is what even a common man would shrink from, how much more a lord of men!" And then the classic exchange: someone in Guan Yu's party said "Land belongs to whoever has the virtue — how can it have a fixed owner?"; Lu Su shouted him down; Guan Yu gestured him away, saying "this is a matter of state, what does this man know?" [18][17].

The crisis was only defused because Cao Cao entered Hanzhong and Liu Bei feared losing Yi. Result: the **Xiang River partition** — Changsha, Jiangxia, Guiyang east to Sun Quan; Nan, Lingling, Wuling west to Liu Bei [2][1]. A truce, not a settlement.

## 4. The alliance's keeper died, and the hardliners took over

Lu Su, who had staked everything on Liu Bei as a buffer against Cao Cao, died in 217 (建安二十二年). Lü Meng succeeded him at Lukou and immediately argued the opposite policy: we need not fear Cao Cao nor rely on Guan Yu, for "Guan Yu and his lord boast of their deceit and force, are double-dealers everywhere, and cannot be treated as bosom friends" — and, decisively, "if we do not go after him while we are strong, once we fall, we will never get another chance" [20].

Sun Quan also rejected Lü Meng's alternative of taking Xuzhou instead, on the sound military reasoning that Xuzhou was flat cavalry country that Cao Cao would contest within ten days, whereas "it is better to take Guan Yu and hold the whole Yangzi" [20].

Meanwhile Sun Quan had already begun realigning: in 217 (建安二十二年) he sent Xu Xiang to Cao Cao to offer submission and "swore to renew a marriage alliance" with him [21].

## 5. The personal grievances

Two fuses lit the powder:

- **The marriage insult.** Sun Quan sent an envoy to seek Guan Yu's daughter as a wife for his son. Guan Yu "reviled and humiliated his envoy and refused the marriage, and Quan was furious" (權大怒, 36-0004). In 《典略》's version, Guan Yu also cursed Sun Quan's envoy as a "minnow" and threatened to destroy him once Fan was taken; Sun Quan, hearing it, "knew he was being held cheap" [28].
- **Guan Yu's own subordinates.** Nan Commandery's governor Mi Fang (at Jiangling) and General Shi Ren (at Gong'an) "had long resented Guan Yu's contempt for them." When Guan Yu marched north, they failed to supply him fully; he said "I'll deal with them when I return," and both feared for their lives. Sun Quan secretly induced them, and they opened the gates [26]. The same pattern held for Pan Jun and Hao Pu, who "were not on good terms with Guan Yu" [34].

## 6. 219: the back-stab

In 219 (建安二十四年) Guan Yu besieged Cao Ren at Fan. Autumn rains flooded the Han River and he captured Yu Jin's seven armies — 30,000 men — and killed Pang De; bandits in Liang, Jia, and Luhun accepted his seals, and "his prestige shook the heartland of China." Cao Cao discussed moving the capital [26].

It was Sima Yi and Jiang Ji who proposed the fatal move: Guan Yu's success is precisely what Sun Quan does not want; "send someone to urge Quan to tread on his heels, and promise to cede the lands south of the Yangzi to enfeoff Quan, and the siege of Fan will dissolve by itself." Cao Cao did it [26]. 《魏略》 records Sun Quan's own letter to Cao Cao "begging to attack Guan Yu to prove his worth," while Cao Cao, wanting the two to bleed each other, had the letter shot into Guan Yu's camp [21].

Lü Meng then stage-managed the operation: he pretended to be gravely ill and was publicly recalled to Jianye; Guan Yu, believing it, drew down his rear garrisons for the front; Lü Meng hid his picked troops in the holds, put men in white to row and dressed as merchants, seized every river watch-post so no word got out, and reached Nan Commandery — where Shi Ren and Mi Fang surrendered [20][33].

Lü Meng's political warfare finished it: he treated Guan Yu's soldiers' families well, let Guan Yu's envoys tour the city and go house to house, so that when the men heard their homes were safe and better treated than before, "the officers and men of Guan Yu had no heart to fight" [35]. Guan Yu fled to Maicheng, then west to Zhangxiang; his troops deserted; Zhu Ran and Pan Zhang cut off his road, and Pan Zhang's commandant Ma Zhong captured him and his son Guan Ping at Zhangxiang in the twelfth month. (《关羽传》 says the killing was at Linju; 《吴主传》 says the capture at Zhangxiang.) The province was his [26][21].

## 7. Why it was always going to happen

- **The alliance had no enforcement mechanism.** As Pei Songzhi observes, "Jing and Wu were outwardly on good terms but inwardly mutually suspicious and on guard" — which is exactly why Sun Quan's strike had to be launched in secret [28].
- **The loan was never repaid, and both sides knew the other would cheat.** Liu Bei's "when Liang is settled" was transparently a stall; Sun Quan's response — appointing his own officials inside Liu Bei's territory — was transparently a provocation.
- **The strategic logic outlived the anti-Cao logic.** Lu Su's premise was that Cao Cao was the existential threat and Liu Bei the necessary buffer. By 217–219, with Cao Cao old, the north busy, and Liu Bei suddenly holding Yi *and* Jing *and* threatening Xiangyang, the buffer had become the greater danger to Sun Quan — the power astride the upper Yangzi.
- **The human factor.** Guan Yu's arrogance — toward Sun Quan's envoy, toward Mi Fang, Shi Ren, Pan Jun, and Hao Pu — converted a strategic decision into an easy one. Sun Quan could not have taken Jing so cheaply against a general whose own subordinates trusted him.

Sun Quan's own epitaph on the matter is in his eulogy of Lu Su: he kept Lu Su's two great services in mind and "forgot his shortcoming" — the shortcoming being the loan of Jing to Liu Bei [13]. The alliance quarreled because it was never an alliance of equals with a shared goal; it was two rivals who both intended to hold the whole river, postponing the collision only as long as Cao Cao made it unwise.

q: Who had the courtesy name Wenze?
reply:
**于禁**（字文則）——曹魏名将，泰山郡钜平县人（《三国志·魏书·张乐于张徐传》）。他早年随鲍信，后归曹操，历任军司马、陷阵都尉、平虏校尉等，以治军严整著称；最出名的事是樊城之败后投降关羽，曹丕后来以此羞辱他，谥为厉侯。

此外，《三国志》及裴注中还记有两位字"文则"的人：
- **吴范**（字文则），会稽上虞人，孙吴的方术之士，以推算历数、占候风气闻名（《吴书·吴范刘惇赵达传》）。
- **严象**（字文则），京兆人，曾任扬州刺史，建安五年被孙策所任庐江太守李术杀害，年三十八（裴松之注引《三辅决录》）。

若你问的是一般所指，通常就是**于禁**。

q: When Liu Bei was gravely ill, Huang Yuan, the Grand Administrator of Hanjia, rebelled and burned Linqiong. How did Yang Hong work out where Huang Yuan would go, and how was he captured?
reply:
## 事情经过

据《三国志·蜀书十一·杨洪传》[1]，及《蜀书二·先主传》[12][13]：

**背景**：刘备称帝后东征孙吴失利，退驻永安。汉嘉太守黄元一向不被诸葛亮喜欢，听说刘备病重，怕将来有后患，便举郡造反，烧了临邛城。当时诸葛亮东下探望刘备病情，成都空虚，黄元因此更加无所忌惮。

**杨洪的判断与部署**：杨洪（时任蜀郡太守一类职务，字季休）当即禀告太子（刘禅），派出太子的亲兵，命将军陈曶、郑绰去讨伐黄元。

**众人的猜测**：众人议论认为，黄元如果不能围攻成都，就应当经由越巂（越囗）去占据南中。

**杨洪的推理**（原文）：
> 「元素信凶暴，無他恩信，何能辦此？不過乘水東下，冀主上平安，面縛歸死；如其有異，奔吳求活耳。敕曶、綽但於南安峽口遮即便得矣。」

意思是：黄元向来凶暴，并没有别的恩德信义，怎么能办成占据南中这种事？他不过是顺水东下——如果主上平安，他就自缚回来请死；如果主上出了变故，就逃奔吴国求活罢了。所以只要命陈曶、郑绰在南安峡口拦截，就能抓到他。

**结果**：陈曶、郑绰依杨洪之言行事，果然活捉了黄元（「果生獲元」）。

《先主传》记章武三年（223）三月，黄元进兵攻临邛县，朝廷派将军陈曶讨伐，黄元军败，顺流下江，被自己的亲兵捆绑，活着送到成都斩首（此处只提陈曶，且说是被其亲兵所缚；杨洪传则说是被陈曶、郑绰生擒）。

## 一点说明

两处记载略有出入：杨洪传强调杨洪料定他必走水路东下、在**南安峡口**设伏生擒；先主传则说他是战败顺流东下、被**自己的亲兵**捆绑送成都斩首。核心情节（杨洪断定黄元不会去南中，只会顺江东下，因而在南安峡口截击）是一致的。

q: How did Xu Zhu realize that Xu Ta and the others were plotting to assassinate Cao Cao? And how did he deal with them?
reply:
**How he found out:** He didn't learn of it through any informant — the plot was betrayed by his own intuition. According to Xu Chu's biography in the *Wei Shu* (《三国志·魏书·许褚传》), Xu Ta (徐他) and other soldiers who regularly attended Cao Cao plotted treason, but because Xu Chu was constantly at Cao Cao's side they were too afraid to act. They therefore waited for a day when Xu Chu was off duty and went in carrying concealed knives. Xu Chu, however, "reached the rest quarters and his heart stirred" (至下舍心动) — he felt uneasy and immediately went back to his guard post. Xu Ta and the others, unaware of this, entered the tent and saw Xu Chu there; they were greatly astonished. Xu Ta's expression changed, Xu Chu noticed it, and at once struck them dead (即击杀他等). Cao Cao thereafter trusted him even more, keeping him at his side coming and going.

Two notes on details:
- Pei Songzhi, in his commentary (in the *San Shaodi ji*, 04-0009n0), refers to the man as **徐佗** rather than 徐他, and praises Xu Chu's instinctive alertness as "loyalty of the highest order," comparing him to Jin Midi (金日磾).
- The text does not give a year for the incident; it is placed after Xu Chu's service at Guandu (官渡), but the exact date is not stated.

q: Which Cavalier Regular Palace Attendant of Wu got drunk and collapsed at the banquet Sun Hao held for Ding Zhong on his return from an embassy to Jin, and was beheaded in the hall on Sun Hao's orders? In which year?
reply:
**王蕃（字永元），公元 266 年（孙吴甘露二年）。**

《三国志·吴书·王楼贺韦华传》所载王蕃本传：

> 甘露二年，丁忠使晋还，皓大会群臣，蕃沉醉顿伏。皓疑而不悦，举蕃出外。顷之请还，酒亦不解。蕃性有威严，行止自若，皓大怒，呵左右于殿下斩之。卫将军滕牧、征西将军留平请，不能得。

（甘露二年，丁忠出使晋国回来，孙皓大会群臣，王蕃喝得大醉伏倒在地。孙皓起疑心而不高兴，命人把王蕃抬出去。不久王蕃请求回席，酒意仍未醒。王蕃生性有威严，举止仍如平常，孙皓大怒，喝令左右在殿下把他斩了。滕牧、留平求情也没能救下。）

几点说明：

- 王蕃此前在孙休时与贺邵、薛莹、虞汜同为**散骑中常侍**（加驸马都尉），孙皓初年又入朝为常侍，正是所问的官职。
- 年份：孙吴甘露二年 = 公元 **266 年**（这一年也是晋泰始二年；丁忠、张俨于宝鼎元年正月奉派吊祭晋文帝司马昭，裴松之指出丁忠从北方回来是在此年春天）。王蕃死时三十九岁。
- 裴注另引《江表传》，说王蕃是被杀于孙皓西巡武昌、欲迁都而大宴群臣之时，因未及回答“射不主皮”之义而被斩于殿上，裴松之指出此与本传不同。

q: How many different people named Zhao Da appear in the Records of the Three Kingdoms, and what did each of them do?
reply:
## Two different people named Zhao Da (趙達) in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*

### 1. Zhao Da, the Wei "school officer" (校事)

A secret-police/oversight official under Cao Cao (魏太祖). He and Lu Hong (盧洪) were appointed as 校事 to spy on and report on the officials:

- **In Gao Rou's biography (魏書 24):** When Cao Cao set up Lu Hong and Zhao Da as 校事 to watch the bureaucracy, Gao Rou protested that such posts betrayed the principle of a ruler trusting his subordinates and that "Zhao Da and the others repeatedly abuse their power and exercise arbitrary rewards and punishments out of personal likes and dislikes." Cao Cao brushed the objection aside (citing Shu Sun Tong's use of "a band of robbers"), but later, when Zhao Da and the others' corrupt pursuit of profit came to light, Cao Cao had them executed as a gesture of apology to Gao Rou.
- **In Xu Miao's biography (魏書 27):** When liquor was officially banned, Xu Miao drank in private until drunk; 校事 Zhao Da questioned him about official business and Xu Miao answered "中聖人" ("I've hit a sage" — a drunkard's slang for clear wine). Zhao Da reported this to Cao Cao, who was furious; only Xianyu Fu's intervention saved Xu Miao from punishment.

(The database initially lists these two citations as separate "Zhao Da" entries, but they are clearly the same man: the 校事 under Cao Cao.)

### 2. Zhao Da, the Wu diviner (吳書 63, in the 吳範劉惇趙達傳)

A native of Henan (河南) who studied under the Han palace attendant Shan Fu (單甫), then crossed the Yangzi because he judged the southeast to hold "royal qi" (王者氣) and a place of refuge. He practiced the "Nine Palaces single-calculation" art (九宮一算之術):

- He was reputed to compute the number of flying locusts, guess hidden objects, and count beans scattered on a mat with uncanny accuracy; he also detected a hidden jar of wine and three catties of venison by manipulating chopsticks, and exposed a "thousand-myriad" figure written on a sealed slip as "having a name but no substance."
- **Under Sun Quan:** Whenever Sun Quan went on campaigns he had Zhao Da make predictions, and they always came out as foretold — but Zhao Da would never reveal his method, so Sun Quan slighted him and his salary and rank never rose. (Pei's note quoting the *Wu Shu* adds that Sun Quan asked him how many years he would reign after becoming emperor, and Zhao Da answered that he would double Han Gaozu's twelve years.)
- **His death:** He calculated the exact year, month and day of his own death; when his wife wept, he recalculated and told her it had been a mistake — then died on schedule. Sun Quan, hearing he had written books, sought them in vain, arrested and questioned his daughter, and had his coffin opened, but found nothing, so the art was lost.
- He is listed among Wu's "men of the arts" (術數) alongside Wu Fan in the appraisal of the Three Rulers of Wu.

The two are unrelated: one was a Wei secret agent executed by Cao Cao, the other a Wu diviner who kept his art secret and died under Sun Quan.

args.query: 趙達

q: What did Liu Bei say to Zhuge Liang when he entrusted his heir to him on his deathbed? How did Zhuge Liang reply? And what instructions did Liu Bei leave for the Later Sovereign?
reply:
## The deathbed scene (章武三年 / 223 CE)

**Location and setting:** In the spring of 章武三年, Liu Bei, gravely ill at 永安 (Yong'an, i.e. 白帝城), summoned Zhuge Liang from Chengdu to entrust him with the aftermath. He died that summer, in the fourth month, aged 63 (《先主传》).

**What Liu Bei said to Zhuge Liang** (《诸葛亮传》, 蜀书五):

> 「君才十倍曹丕，必能安國，終定大事。若嗣子可輔，輔之；如其不才，君可自取。」
>
> "Your ability is ten times that of Cao Pi; you will surely be able to secure the state and in the end accomplish the great undertaking. If my heir is worth supporting, support him; if he has no ability, you may take [the throne] yourself."

**Zhuge Liang's reply:**

> 「臣敢竭股肱之力，效忠貞之節，繼之以死！」
>
> "How would I dare not exhaust the strength of arm and thigh, and render a loyal and steadfast integrity, continuing it unto death!"

**Instructions for the Later Sovereign:** Liu Bei also issued an edict admonishing Liu Shan:

> 「汝與丞相從事，事之如父。」
>
> "You are to serve the Chancellor [in government]; treat him as you would your father."

## Additional material from the 《诸葛亮集》 (裴注引, in 《先主传》)

Pei Songzhi's note preserves the fuller text of Liu Bei's testamentary edict to the Later Sovereign. In it he says he is over sixty and has no regrets, only concern for "you brothers"; he reports that an envoy (射君) told him Zhuge Liang praised Liu Shan's intelligence and progress beyond expectation; then the famous lines:

> 「勿以惡小而為之，勿以善小而不為。惟賢惟德，能服於人。汝父德薄，勿效之。」
>
> "Do not do a thing because it is a small evil; do not fail to do a thing because it is a small good. Only worthiness and virtue can win men's submission. Your father was of thin virtue—do not imitate him."

He also advises reading the *Han shu* and *Li ji*, and in spare time the various philosophers, the *Liu Tao* and *Shang Jun shu*; he notes that Zhuge Liang had finished copying the *Shenzi*, *Hanfeizi*, *Guanzi* and *Liu Tao* for him, but the copy was lost on the road, so he should seek them again himself.

Finally, at the point of death he called in the Prince of Lu (鲁王) and told him: "After I die, you brothers are to treat the Chancellor as a father; you need only serve together with the Chancellor."

## A note on interpretation

The phrase 「如其不才，君可自取」 is genuinely in Chen Shou's text. Pei Songzhi appends Sun Sheng's sharp criticism of it [21]: Sun Sheng argues that a true trust in a loyal and worthy man needs no such words, and that if the recipient were unworthy the words only open the road to usurpation — so Liu Bei's command was "the most disorderly" of acts, and only luck (Liu Shan's pliancy and Zhuge Liang's authority) prevented suspicion and trouble.

The 副手 arrangement is worth noting: 《先主传》 records that the entrustment was to Zhuge Liang as principal with 尚书令李严 as deputy (「託孤於丞相亮，尚書令李嚴為副」), and Li Yan was made 中都护, commanding internal and external military affairs, stationed at Yong'an (《李严传》).
